coreField.label: Globalisation and global interconnection: global flows of goods, people, cultural norms and ideas across the economy, politics, culture, law and environment; how local developments change the world and global processes reshape local communities; the obligations that globalisation creates towards other people; and stakeholder analysis, introduced in the programme's opening Introduction to Global Studies semester.

Environment and economy: key environmental discourses, how the environment is valued socially and economically across time, place and scale, the basic principles of environmental economics and policy, policy instruments and collective arrangements for managing the environment, and analysis and visualisation of country-level emissions and economic data, as taught in the second semester Environment & Economy.

Migration and citizenship: core concepts and theories of migration and citizenship, legal categories and channels for mobility, individuals' motivations and aspirations, and the legal, psychological and social consequences of mobility for global citizenship and inclusion, as taught in the third semester Migration & Citizenship.

Tolerance, beliefs and global health: how beliefs and tolerance are constructed and affect global change, studied through social psychology, religious and cultural studies, global health and anthropology, with flows of ideologies, identities and ideas, social differentiation, social cohesion and the analysis of cases of (in)tolerance, as taught in the fourth semester Tolerance & Beliefs.

Peace and justice: mutual obligations as an ingredient of justice, how just and peaceful societies handle conflicting obligations, and how globalisation flows apply to fundamental rights, legal practice, economic development and political institutions, with a field study, as taught in the fifth semester Peace & Justice; together with the international relations, global governance, human-rights and international-law strands that the programme names among its disciplines.

21st Century Learning and stakeholder projects: working with an external stakeholder to define, analyse and solve a local or global learning dilemma, project management and analytical insight, global learning topics, and a personal development plan, as taught in the sixth semester.

Research methods, data and thesis training: a methods practical in every semester, data collection, analysis and presentation, qualitative and quantitative methods learned in the first two years for the field study, visualisation of processes, flows and results, and an interdisciplinary bachelor thesis integrating at least two disciplines.

Foreign-language training in the first two years: a foreign language other than English or the student's native language, chosen from Arabic, Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish.
Economics and political economy among the disciplines that the programme integrates, including the economics of the global economy, trade and development.

History, philosophy, sociology and anthropology among the humanities and social-science disciplines that the programme integrates, including the history and philosophy behind global problems and sociology and social change.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Alternative 2 changes the organising discipline: the closest match is a social-science programme in which environment is one of six global themes (Climate Change, Governance of Sustainability, two economics courses and Social Movements & Environmental Justice), whereas this programme makes the environmental and sustainability sciences its core. It shares only nine of 24 courses with Alternative 1 (Personal & Professional Development, Climate Change, Governance of Sustainability, Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Research Methods & Statistics, Introduction to Data Science, Social Movements & Environmental Justice and Ethics), so each programme has fifteen courses (112.5 EC) that the other lacks, well above the 30 EC floor. The fifteen different courses are consequences of the concept: Earth-system, climate-risk, energy, circular-economy, water, resource, biodiversity and Earth-science courses with their gateway courses replace the sociology, political science, history, law, psychology and public-health courses that the closest match uses for migration, tolerance and beliefs, and peace and justice, and Public Economics and Communicating the Climate Crisis replace the social-theory and media courses.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Law, Society & Justice (semester 1) precedes Introduction to Public International Law (semester 4) and Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes International Macroeconomics (semester 3). Every course is placed in a semester in which it is planned. Advisory progression is respected where the planned semesters allow: Introduction to Sociology, Law, Society & Justice, History of Empires and Climate Change open the programme, Research Methods & Statistics and Qualitative Research Methodology come in year 1, Introduction to Sociology precedes the 300-level New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory (which builds on it), social psychology and international relations theory precede the 300-level Peace & Conflict and Youth Resilience to Extremism, and the justice-oriented courses Social Movements & Environmental Justice, Peace & Conflict and Ethics are placed in the final semester in line with the Peace & Justice theme. Introduction to Economics now precedes International Macroeconomics; History of Empires moves to Year3autumn. This improves advisory sequencing without inventing a new prerequisite.

progressionAssessment.rationale: Every formal prerequisite is scheduled in an earlier semester: Sustainability Essentials I (semester 1) precedes Sustainability Essentials II and Earth System Science Tools (semester 2) and Environmental Biogeochemistry (semester 5); Sustainability Essentials II (semester 2) precedes Renewable System Design (semester 4) and R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation (semester 5); Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes International Macroeconomics (semester 3) and Public Economics (semester 4). Every course is placed in a semester in which it is planned, including the single-semester Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy (semester 3), Living with Water (semester 4) and Public Economics (semester 4). Advisory progression is respected: Climate Change, Dynamic Earth and Introduction to Economics open the programme, the gateway courses precede the 300-level energy, circular-economy and biogeochemistry courses, and the applied Research in a Sustainable Delta and the climate-communication, ethics and environmental-justice courses come in the last year.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two UCR alternatives are defensible and production stopped at two. Alternative 1 owns sixteen generator-eligible rows as the target's own core: interconnected global challenges and the effects of globalisation on local communities (5991, 5992), migration and citizenship (5994, 5999), social exclusion and belonging and tolerance and belief (5995, 6000), responsible solutions to global problems (5997), learning and social change in the twenty-first century (6002), political economy and development and international relations and global governance (6003, 6004), anthropology and cultural diversity (6007), the history and philosophy behind global problems (6008), public health and psychological perspectives (6009, 6010), sociology and social change (6011) and Dutch language (6019). UCR covers most of these through sociology, history, politics, health and psychology courses, but has no migration, anthropology, religious-studies or education course, so those rows are approached only indirectly and with stated limits. Three candidate directions were assessed. The first, climate, sustainability and environmental science with economics and policy (5993, 5998, 6005, 6012, supported by 6013), is a coherent direction evidenced by the programme's second semester and four direct interests; the closest match holds only four environment and economics courses while UCR has a large environmental and sustainability cluster, so a different curriculum follows, passes the 30 EC floor with 15 different courses each and is included as Alternative 2. The second, human rights, international law and global justice (5996, 6001, 6006, supported by 6014), is coherent, but the UCR courses that implement it, Law, Society & Justice, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy, Introduction to Public International Law, Peace & Conflict, Social Movements & Environmental Justice and Ethics, are all already in Alternative 1; the remaining UCR law courses (criminal, comparative constitutional, private and EU law) have no demonstrated link to the target's evidence, so a third programme could only reuse the closest-match courses or add unevidenced national-law courses, and the candidate is rejected as not-substantively-distinct. The third, modern foreign-language study beyond Dutch (Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish; 6017, 6018, 6020 to 6025), is evidenced by the programme's language requirement but UCR's course database contains no course in any of these languages, so no 24-course programme can be built around it and it is rejected as not-feasible. Curricular topics (6013 to 6016) only support the core and the outcome interests (6026 to 6034) are search-only and generate nothing.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both develop academic reading, writing, reflection and interpersonal skills. Maastricht embeds these in global citizenship and problem-based learning; the credits and scope differ.
Both teach inferential statistics, estimation and hypothesis testing. UCR provides a general methods foundation; Maastricht applies statistics to environmental and economic datasets.
Both teach data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation through practical analysis. Maastricht uses Python; UCR uses its own tools and projects rather than the same programming curriculum.
Both address policy tools for environmental problems and the roles of public and private actors. Maastricht integrates climate science and economics; UCR concentrates on sustainability governance.

Refugee law provides a specific overlap with Maastricht’s legal categories and mobility channels. UCR is a broad public-international-law course; Maastricht integrates economics, psychology and the full migration trajectory.

Both analyse conflict and ways to build peaceful societies. Maastricht combines this with justice and preparation for the field study; UCR focuses on conflict causation, transformation and peacebuilding.

Both examine how social processes connect people and societies. Sociology supplies a disciplinary foundation; Maastricht explicitly integrates theories and histories of globalisation across disciplines.

Both develop qualitative research design and data analysis in a research project. Maastricht specifically trains semi-structured migration interviews; UCR offers a broader qualitative research process.

Both provide language study when Dutch is selected as a non-native language. UCR’s single introductory Dutch course does not reproduce the four-semester Maastricht language track or its level requirement.
Both examine environmental discourse and how power shapes environmental communication. The UCR course analyses media and arguments; Maastricht explicitly trains qualitative discourse analysis.

notes.text: Maastricht integrates six themes with methods, language study, projects, a field study and a compulsory final thesis. The UCR alternatives organise related subjects in separate courses. The environmental programme develops one direction more deeply and covers fewer of the other themes.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht Global Studies combines social sciences, humanities, environmental science and health to examine how global processes affect local communities. Its six themes include environment and economy, migration, beliefs, peace and learning.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR programme studies global challenges across several fields. The second concentrates on environmental science, economics and policy. Neither reproduces Maastricht’s integrated semesters, full language track, field study or compulsory thesis. Blank cells identify content without a sufficiently specific counterpart.

curriculum.limitation: This 180-EC pathway uses Peace & Justice and its field study, rather than the alternative minor. Language study spans four semesters; students must meet the required language level. Attendance and chronological progression rules apply. The 20-EC thesis is an individual interdisciplinary research project assessed by two graders.

componentNotes.s4-proj: The current course catalogue calls this 4-EC project Preparing for the Field. The adopted regulations retain the title shown here.
